newsitem.title: UK: Dlr springs to new peaks as Buba keeps powder dry.
newsitem.headline: Dlr springs to new peaks as Buba keeps powder dry.

text.p: The dollar sprang to its highest in nearly eight years against the mark on Tuesday after the Bundesbank opted to keep its powder dry and refrained from engineering higher money-market rates in its currency's defence.
Expectations persist that the Bundesbank will allow its securities repurchase rate to drift up from a record low of 3.0 percent if the mark extends its two-year slide.
Dollar bulls are, however, expecting the fragility of Germany's economic recovery to give them the edge in any battle of wills with the German central bank.

"The Bundesbank has little room to manoeuvre to counteract the weakness of the mark and as soon as they switch to setting variable-rate repos, they will have shot all their ammunition," said Brian Martin, currency strategist at BZW in London.
"This is already the third largest appreciation in the dollar's floating-rate history but it looks like we will break above 1.90 (marks) and eventually 2.0," he said.

The dollar topped 1.88 marks for the first time since October 1989 to rise as high as 1.8805. It was at 1.8798/03 at 1045 GMT from 1.8618 late Monday in New York. Dollar/yen was at 118.34/41 from 118.06 yesterday.

Expectations the Bundesbank will allow rates to drift higher have intensified as the mark slid nearly eight percent against the dollar in the past month alone and tumbled to five-year lows on trade-weighted terms.

Willi Leibfritz, economist at Germany's Ifo research institute, said on Tuesday that dollar gains above 1.90 marks would "set alarm bells ringing in Frankfurt" and prompt the central bank to take action.
"If the bells are not already ringing, their alarm system can't be very good," said David Bloom, strategist at HSBC James Capel, who is targeting a move to 2.0 marks.
"The dollar is going up, up and away and the question is what can the Bundesbank realistically do about it. The economy just doesn't need higher rates."
The still-fragile nature of German economic recovery contrasts with the strong pace of growth the U.S. economy has managed to sustain in recent quarters without stoking inflation.
Friday's July jobless report was even strong enough to revive speculation that the target Fed funds rate could be raised from 5.5 percent in the next month or two.
"The expectations of higher U.S.rates and strong growth are also giving the dollar a fillip," said BZW's Martin.

With economic fundamentals on their side, traders are getting bolder about testing how far Germany and other members of the Group of Seven leading industrial nations will allow the dollar to rally against the mark.

The G7 called for currency stability in February and again in April, saying that misalignments in major exchange rates seen in 1995 had been corrected. But analysts and traders expect they will be wary of launching intervention to back up their words as long as economic fundamentals argue for a stronger dollar.
"Intervention will just be a way of giving away free money given the economic outlook," said Bloom at HSBC James Capel.

Add persistent expectations that European economic and monetary union will be launched by a broad group of countries to this picture and there is little to deter dollar bulls for the time being, analysts said.

"In the current environment it is just so easy to latch on to factors that work towards mark selling," said Junpei Yamamoto, head of foreign exchange at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi. "The market now has 1.90 in its sights."
